title: Email overload for consultants on Mac: triage a big inbox in Outlook
metaTitle: Email overload for consultants: triage a big inbox on Mac
description: Email overload for consultants: a practical Mac routine to triage and reply to a large inbox, using Outlook and Apple Mail tools you already have.
intro: Email overload for consultants means more messages than you can answer, and too little quiet time to answer them. This guide shows how to triage a big inbox on a Mac, using Focused Inbox, rules and views you already have in Outlook, Apple Mail or Gmail.
tldr: Email is a big share of a consultant's week. Microsoft's 2023 survey puts the heaviest email users at 8.8 hours a week.
Start with Focused Inbox, then add a short rules list. Both are free and sit in menus you may never have opened.
Check mail in fixed windows. One study linked checking three times a day with lower stress.
Lazur can point, guide, explain and draft. It does not sort, click or send for you.

blocks.text: Email takes a large share of a consultant's week. Microsoft's Work Trend Index surveyed 31,000 full-time workers in 31 markets in early 2023. Email took about 15% of the average person's Microsoft 365 time, in a breakdown that also covered meetings and chat. The heaviest email users, the top 25%, spend 8.8 hours a week on email.
What the 15% and 8.8 hours do not tell you

Those numbers describe the average knowledge worker, not a consultant. They also come from a 2023 survey, so your week may look different. The 15% is a share of app time, not a count of emails or hours spent on them.

A better test is your own week. Note how long you spend in your mail app each day for one full working week. Include reading time, not only replies. Then compare your total with 8.8 hours. If you are above that, triage is worth an afternoon of setup.
What an overloaded inbox costs in money

The Bureau of Labor Statistics reports a median pay of $48.97 an hour for management analysts, as of May 2025. Consultants do not all hold that job title, so treat the wage as a proxy. Multiply 8.8 hours by $48.97 and you get about $431 a week.

Your real cost depends on your billing rate and on how many of those hours could have been billed. Some email is client work. Some is noise. The useful question is which hours you could hand to someone else or cut entirely.

blocks.title: Use the $431 carefully
blocks.text: The $431 figure multiplies a 2023 survey number by a proxy wage. Use it to decide where your time goes. Do not use it to price a proposal or argue a fee with a client.
Set up Focused Inbox in Outlook for Mac

Focused Inbox is the fastest change you can make, and it costs nothing. It splits your inbox into two tabs, Focused and Other. Turn it on before you build rules, so you can see how Outlook sorts your mail on its own.

items: Open Outlook for Mac and look at the View tab in the ribbon.
Choose Turn on Focused Inbox. Your inbox splits into Focused and Other tabs.
Open the Other tab and scan it once for messages that matter, such as a new client who landed there by mistake.
Open the Message menu on a misfiled message. Choose the option that moves future messages from that sender too.

blocks.text: Check the Other tab once a day. Do not treat it as a trash folder. Important messages from new senders can land there, and a missed reply costs more than a quick scan.

blocks.title: Check your Outlook version
blocks.text: Microsoft says support for legacy Outlook for Mac ends in October 2026. If your menu shows an Organize tab with a Focused inbox option, you run the legacy app. Update before you build habits around it.
Build Outlook rules that sort mail before you read it

Microsoft says you can only create server rules in Outlook for Mac now, because client rules are no longer supported. To start, open Outlook > Settings > Rules, then choose + Add Rule. Pick a condition and an action, then save.

Rules run from top to bottom. The Stop processing more rules option is on by default, so a message that matches an early rule can skip the rules below it. Read your list from the top each time you add a rule.

items: Newsletters: sender matches the newsletter's domain, action moves it to a Newsletters folder.
Automated alerts: subject contains the tool's name, action moves it to a folder you check once a day.
Your biggest client: sender matches the client's domain, action moves it to a client folder you open first.

blocks.text: Microsoft's page mentions a Run rule now option for applying a rule to mail you already have. It does not say how far back the rule reaches. Test on one folder first, and check what moved before you trust it.

blocks.caption: Views change what you see. Rules change where mail goes.

blocks.text: Start with views before rules. A view moves nothing, so a mistake costs you nothing. A rule that moves mail can hide a message you need, and you may not notice for days.
How Smart Mailboxes work in Apple Mail

Open Mailbox > New Smart Mailbox in Apple Mail. Set the conditions, then choose whether any or all of them must match. For example, build one Smart Mailbox that collects mail from your main clients. Set it to match any condition so one view gathers every client thread.

Smart Mailboxes gather matching messages from other mailboxes into one view. They do not move mail. Deleting a Smart Mailbox does not delete its emails, so you can test one safely. Edit it later with Mailbox > Edit Smart Mailbox.
Gmail filters for consultants who live in Gmail

Click Show search options in the Gmail search bar. Enter your criteria, such as a sender or a phrase in the subject. Click Create filter, then choose an action, such as applying a label or archiving the message.

Manage filters under Settings > See all settings > Filters and Blocked Addresses. Gmail's help page does not say whether a new filter applies to mail already in your account. Check your inbox after you save one, and test it on a single sender first.
Stop checking email all day

Kushlev and Dunn studied 124 adults. In one condition, people checked email three times a day for a week. The study linked that habit with lower stress than usual checking. Many participants found the limit hard to keep, according to the summary of the paper.

Try a softer version. Pick windows that fit your client calendar, such as late morning, after lunch and before you log off. Close the mail app in between, and turn off the Dock badge if it keeps pulling your eye.
Tell key clients your reply windows once, in a short note. Then you can answer urgent messages quickly without watching the inbox all day. Urgent should mean a named deadline, not a new message.

blocks.title: Leave the 23-minute number out
blocks.text: You will see a claim that it takes 23 minutes to refocus after an interruption. That figure traces to a 2006 interview with Gloria Mark, not to her research papers. Do not quote it in a client deck.
What the interruption studies actually found

In a 2005 CHI study, Gloria Mark and colleagues observed 24 information workers over about 700 hours at one financial services company. People worked about 11 minutes on a task before switching. 57% of those stretches were interrupted.

A 2008 lab study used 48 German students on a simulated email task. Interrupted participants worked faster and kept their quality. They still reported more stress, frustration, time pressure and effort. Speed is not the whole cost. The stress is part of it too.
A four-pass routine for a big inbox
Triage works better as passes than as one long read. Each pass has one job. Give the routine a fixed block of time, and stop when the block ends, even if the inbox still looks full.

items: Pass one: scan senders and subjects only. Move anything that needs no action into a folder you check later.
Pass two: answer quick messages now, while the thread is fresh. If a reply needs real thought, flag it and move on.
Pass three: put real work on your calendar as a time block. A message is not handled until it has a time next to it.
Pass four: clear the noise. Unsubscribe from newsletters you never open, and block senders who never matter.

blocks.text: Edge cases need their own rule. A long thread with many people often needs a call, not another email. Reply once with a time, then move the thread out of the inbox. Also check automatic replies from clients, since an out-of-office note can hide a real request. You can [block a sender in Outlook](/how-to/block-a-sender-in-outlook) when the noise comes from one address.
Reply faster with templates and a request tracker

Keep a short set of reply templates in a plain text file. Cover the replies you write most, such as a meeting request, a status update and a polite decline. Paste one, change a line, and send. Templates save time only if they still sound like you.

Track open requests in one place. In a spreadsheet, make a table with columns for client, request, due date and status. If you use [Excel for consultants](/for/consultants/excel), a table with filters works well. Sort by due date each morning.
You can also dictate a reply. Hold fn and speak. Dictation puts clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app, so you can answer a long message out loud and read it back before you send.
Client data and AI tools

blocks.title: Check your firm's rules first
blocks.text: If a message holds client data, follow your employer's rules before you share it with any AI tool. Consultants often sign confidentiality terms. Ask your firm which tools are allowed for client work.

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold ⌥ ⌘. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so they can answer. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models. Your firm's policy still comes first.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur helps with the parts of triage that involve finding and writing. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask where Focused Inbox is. Lazur points and draws a circle around the control. Ask it to walk you through a rule, and it guides you one click at a time.

Lazur does not sort your inbox. It does not move messages, send replies or click buttons for you. Keep your own routine, and use Lazur for setup questions and for drafting the wording of a reply that you then read.
Mistakes that make inbox overload worse

items: Building a long rules list in one sitting. When a message disappears, you cannot tell which rule moved it.
Forgetting that rules run top to bottom, and that Stop processing more rules is on by default.
Treating the Other tab as a trash folder. Check it once a day, and read the subjects.
Using the 23-minute figure to justify ignoring email. Use the studies instead, with their limits.
Skipping the test. Run each rule on one sender, then check what happened before you trust it.

blocks.text: Where to start this week

Start with Focused Inbox, then add one rule, then set reply windows. Change one thing at a time, so you can tell what helped. faq.question: Does Focused Inbox hide email I need?
faq.answer: Focused Inbox splits your inbox into two tabs, Focused and Other. Messages still live in the inbox, just across two tabs. Check the Other tab once a day, and use the Message menu to move a message to the right tab.

faq.question: Why did my Outlook rule miss an email?
faq.answer: Check the order first. Rules run from top to bottom, and Stop processing more rules is on by default. Then check that the condition matches the sender or subject you expect. Test with one message before you trust a rule.

faq.question: Is the 23-minute refocus figure from research?
faq.answer: No. The figure traces to a 2006 Gallup Business Journal interview with Gloria Mark. It is not in the research papers it is usually credited to, including her 2005 and 2008 CHI studies.

faq.question: Does checking email less really reduce stress?
faq.answer: One study suggests it can. Kushlev and Dunn studied 124 adults, and checking three times a day linked to lower stress. Stress was self-reported, and the summary gives no effect size, so treat it as a hint.

faq.question: Can I use Lazur on messages with client data?
faq.answer: Follow your employer's rules first. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold ⌥ ⌘. Audio and screenshots go to AI providers to answer you. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models.

faq.question: Does Lazur sort or send emails for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur points at things, explains them out loud, guides you one click at a time, and drafts or types text. It does not click buttons, move messages or send replies. You stay in control of every send.

faq.question: Is Gmail triage different from Outlook triage?
faq.answer: The ideas match. Gmail uses filters, made with Show search options and Create filter, and managed under Settings > See all settings > Filters and Blocked Addresses. Outlook uses Focused Inbox and rules. Check each help page for how old mail is handled.

costs.title: Hours you do not get back
costs.text: Microsoft's 2023 survey says the top 25% of email users spend 8.8 hours a week on email. Every hour spent sorting is an hour not spent on the client work you were hired to do.

costs.title: Money, roughly
costs.text: At the median pay for management analysts, $48.97 an hour in May 2025, 8.8 hours is about $431 a week. That is a proxy, not your billing rate, but it shows the scale of the problem.

costs.title: Focus and attention
costs.text: A 2005 CHI study found people worked about 11 minutes on a task before switching. 57% of those stretches were interrupted. Each check can break a stretch of deep work you were building.

costs.title: Stress
costs.text: A study of 124 adults found that checking email three times a day linked to lower stress than usual checking. Many participants found that limit hard to keep, so expect some friction at first.

costs.title: Replies that turn into follow-ups
costs.text: A message left for days often comes back as a follow-up, then a complaint. Each follow-up adds more mail to the pile you already have to read, which makes the next triage session longer.

causes.title: Every sender feels urgent
causes.text: Clients, partners, vendors and your own team all write to the same inbox. Nothing in the inbox ranks their needs. The newest message looks most urgent, even when a slower message matters more.

causes.title: Email doubles as a task list
causes.text: Many people keep requests as unread messages. An unread message is not a plan. Without a flag or a calendar block, a request stays in the inbox until someone chases it, and the pile grows.

causes.title: Views and rules never got set up
causes.text: Focused Inbox and rules are free, but most people never open the menus that hold them. The default inbox treats every message the same, so the pile keeps growing by default.

causes.title: Long threads with many people
causes.text: A single thread grows with every reply, and each reply goes to everyone on it. Short replies like thanks add mail that nobody needs, and the thread takes up space in the inbox.

causes.title: Checking all day
causes.text: When you check mail the moment it arrives, the inbox never closes. Each check restarts the reading. The batch-checking study found lower stress when people checked less often, not less work done.

fixes.title: Turn on Focused Inbox first
fixes.text: In Outlook for Mac, go to View > Turn on Focused Inbox, or use the View tab in the new app. Scan the Other tab once a day, and move misfiled senders with the Message menu. It costs nothing and takes a few minutes.

fixes.title: Keep a short rules list
fixes.text: Open Outlook > Settings > Rules, then choose + Add Rule. Start with newsletters and automated alerts. Test each rule on a few messages, and keep the list short so you can read it from top to bottom.

fixes.title: Use one view for each client
fixes.text: In Apple Mail, use Mailbox > New Smart Mailbox to gather matching mail in one view without moving it. In Gmail, use Show search options, then Create filter, to label mail from a set of clients.

fixes.title: Batch your checks
fixes.text: Pick fixed windows for mail, such as late morning and after lunch. Close the mail app between them. The stress result came from checking three times a day, so start there and adjust to your client calendar.

fixes.title: Unsubscribe and block
fixes.text: Unsubscribe from newsletters you never open, and block senders who never matter. Stop the next message first. Clearing the whole backlog is optional, and it takes much longer than stopping the flow.

fixes.title: Use templates and a request tracker
fixes.text: Keep a short set of reply templates in a plain text file. Track open requests in a spreadsheet with client, request, due date and status columns. Sort by due date each morning, before you open the inbox.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Measure the week
plan.text: Note how long you spend in your mail app for one working day. Write the number down. Compare it with the 8.8 hours in the Microsoft survey to see where you stand.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Turn on Focused Inbox
plan.text: In Outlook for Mac, open View > Turn on Focused Inbox, or use the View tab in the new app. Scan the Other tab once and move any misfiled senders.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Add a few rules
plan.text: Create rules for newsletters, automated alerts and your biggest client. Test each one on a single sender. Keep the list short so you can read it from top to bottom.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Set reply windows
plan.text: Choose fixed times for mail, such as late morning and after lunch. Tell key clients once. Close the mail app between windows and notice how the day feels.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Review and clear
plan.text: Unsubscribe from newsletters you never open. Block senders who never matter. Check the Other tab, then compare your mail time with what you measured on Day 1.
